taxonomy.name: Ideology registry
taxonomy.description: Canonical ideology and political-judgment construct registry

ontology.name: Ideology ontology
ontology.description: Versioned conceptual graph for ideology records

constructs.name: Authority Legitimacy
constructs.description: Whether a central institution holding exclusive power over law and force needs special justification, or may be presumed legitimate.
constructs.negativePole: Authority requires constant justification
constructs.positivePole: Centralized authority is presumptively legitimate

constructs.name: Property Legitimacy
constructs.description: How strong a moral claim private ownership of productive assets carries relative to collective or common claims.
constructs.negativePole: Collective claims are at least as strong as private title
constructs.positivePole: Private property rights are strongly legitimate

constructs.name: Conceptions of Liberty
constructs.description: Whether political freedom is understood mainly as being left unimpeded or also as having the practical independence and protection from arbitrary power needed to act.
constructs.negativePole: Freedom also depends on autonomy, capacity, or protection from domination
constructs.positivePole: Freedom mainly means absence of interference

constructs.name: Formal vs Substantive Equality
constructs.description: Whether justice primarily requires equal legal status and rules or also requires reducing material disparities.
constructs.negativePole: Equal legal status and rules are the main requirement
constructs.positivePole: Reducing material disparities is also a central requirement

constructs.name: Political Community Boundary
constructs.description: Whether moral and political obligations are concentrated within a particular community or extend universally.
constructs.negativePole: Special obligations to compatriots may outweigh duties to outsiders
constructs.positivePole: Nationality does not limit people’s basic moral standing

constructs.name: Moral Traditionalism
constructs.description: Whether inherited norms around personal and family conduct deserve deference, or whether a wide range of personal moral choices should be left open.
constructs.negativePole: Pluralism and permissiveness in personal morality are appropriate
constructs.positivePole: A traditional, settled moral order should be upheld

constructs.name: Anti-Domination vs Hierarchy Acceptance
constructs.description: Whether established hierarchy is entitled to continuing deference or must remain open to challenge and effective checks.
constructs.negativePole: Established hierarchies may remain legitimate without continuing contestability
constructs.positivePole: Hierarchy requires continuing checks, contestability, and justification

constructs.name: Ecocentric vs Anthropocentric Priority
constructs.description: Whether the nonhuman environment carries moral weight in its own right, or whether nature is properly valued chiefly as a resource for human flourishing.
constructs.negativePole: Human welfare and productive use of nature take priority
constructs.positivePole: The natural world has standing independent of human use

constructs.name: Pacifism vs Conditional Use of Force
constructs.description: Whether military force can ever be morally justified; this does not measure support for frequent intervention or military dominance.
constructs.negativePole: Military force is never morally justified
constructs.positivePole: Military force can be morally justified under specified conditions

constructs.name: Secularism vs Religious Public Order
constructs.description: Whether government and public institutions should be neutral with respect to religion, or may legitimately promote and reflect religious values.
constructs.negativePole: Public institutions should be neutral among religions and non-religion
constructs.positivePole: Public life should reflect a religious moral order

constructs.name: Market-Process Confidence
constructs.description: Empirical confidence that decentralized price-driven exchange tends to allocate resources effectively.
constructs.negativePole: Markets routinely misallocate resources or produce harmful outcomes
constructs.positivePole: Markets generally coordinate information and resources well

constructs.name: State-Capacity Confidence
constructs.description: Empirical confidence in the administrative capability of state institutions to carry out ambitious programs.
constructs.negativePole: States usually fail to execute complex tasks well
constructs.positivePole: States can competently execute complex policy

constructs.name: Public-Choice Skepticism
constructs.description: Empirical expectation that public institutions are bent toward the interests of insiders, regulators, or organized lobbies rather than the public.
constructs.negativePole: Public institutions usually overcome self-interest and capture
constructs.positivePole: Public institutions are often shaped by self-interest and capture

constructs.name: Democratic Confidence
constructs.description: Empirical confidence that majoritarian democratic processes reliably produce good collective decisions.
constructs.negativePole: Voters are often manipulable or poorly informed
constructs.positivePole: Voters generally deliberate well and reach sound decisions

constructs.name: Expert Confidence
constructs.description: Empirical confidence that technical or professional expertise, once given authority, tends to produce better outcomes rather than self-serving or insulated decision-making.
constructs.negativePole: Expert bodies tend to cartelize or detach from public accountability
constructs.positivePole: Delegating decisions to experts generally improves governance

constructs.name: Cultural Plasticity vs Persistence
constructs.description: Empirical belief about how malleable cultural patterns, norms, and behavior are in response to law and policy.
constructs.negativePole: Culture and norms are path-dependent and resist deliberate policy change
constructs.positivePole: Culture and norms respond readily to policy and institutional design

constructs.name: Coordination Optimism
constructs.description: Empirical expectation about whether decentralized, voluntary arrangements between individuals and groups tend to succeed or fail absent a central coordinator.
constructs.negativePole: Decentralized coordination often fails without central direction
constructs.positivePole: Decentralized coordination often succeeds without central direction

constructs.name: Centralization Preference
constructs.description: Whether power and policymaking should be concentrated or dispersed across smaller units.
constructs.negativePole: Authority and decision-making should be decentralized
constructs.positivePole: Authority and decision-making should be centralized

constructs.name: Reform vs Revolution
constructs.description: Whether desired change should be pursued by reforming current institutions or by replacing them outright.
constructs.negativePole: Change should work through existing institutions
constructs.positivePole: Existing institutions should be ruptured and replaced

constructs.name: Gradualism vs Immediatism
constructs.description: Whether favored reforms should be sequenced slowly to manage transition costs, or enacted at once.
constructs.negativePole: Change should be phased in gradually
constructs.positivePole: Change should be implemented immediately

constructs.name: State Action vs Exit
constructs.description: Whether the preferred remedy to a given problem runs through state provision or through opting out into voluntary alternatives.
constructs.negativePole: Problems are best solved by exit into private or counter-institutional alternatives
constructs.positivePole: Problems are best solved through state action and public provision

constructs.name: Electoralism vs Direct Action
constructs.description: Whether favored strategies for change rely on formal political and legal processes or on direct action that bypasses them.
constructs.negativePole: Change should be pursued through direct action outside formal channels
constructs.positivePole: Change should be pursued through electoral and institutional channels

constructs.name: Compromise vs Persistence
constructs.description: Whether achieving partial gains through negotiated compromise is preferable to holding out for a fuller, uncompromised outcome.
constructs.negativePole: Ideological commitments should be held firm despite opposition
constructs.positivePole: Practical compromise with opponents is usually worthwhile

constructs.name: Coercion Strategy
constructs.description: Whether the use of coercive or forceful tactics, beyond ordinary persuasion and lawful process, can be justified to advance favored political ends.
constructs.negativePole: Change should be pursued only through peaceful, non-coercive strategies
constructs.positivePole: Change may be pursued through coercive strategies in some circumstances

constructs.name: Regulation vs Deregulation
constructs.description: Whether the preferred policy direction is to reduce regulatory constraint or to add and strengthen oversight.
constructs.negativePole: Regulatory constraints should be reduced or simplified
constructs.positivePole: Regulatory constraints and oversight should be strengthened

constructs.name: Redistribution vs Predistribution
constructs.description: Whether the preferred remedy for unmet material need is transferring resources after the fact or changing the rules that shape market outcomes beforehand.
constructs.negativePole: Underlying rules governing markets should be altered before distribution occurs
constructs.positivePole: Material need is best addressed by redistributing after market outcomes occur

items.prompt: Do you agree that a political order is more legitimate when people can refuse its services without being treated as criminals?
Do you agree that monopoly government is morally suspect even when it produces some useful public goods?
Do you agree that emergency conditions do not by themselves create unlimited political authority?
Do you agree that when existing institutions are unjust, obedience deserves a weaker presumption than peaceful resistance?
Do you agree that political authority should be judged by consent and exit, not merely by elections or inherited borders?
Do you agree that in U.S. metropolitan police-service comparisons, more autonomous service providers were not associated with lower efficiency and were sometimes associated with higher efficiency?
Do you agree that in documented common-pool and polycentric settings, durable cooperation has relied on predictable rules, monitoring, graduated sanctions, and accessible conflict resolution?
Do you agree that reform authority should be distributed across independently accountable institutions rather than concentrated in one national body?
Do you agree that abolition of state functions should be sequenced around credible replacement institutions, not slogans?
Do you agree that civil-liberties safeguards should be enacted before an agency receives additional enforcement powers?
Do you agree that enforcement agencies should be divided among independently accountable bodies rather than placed under one executive authority?
Do you agree that a constitution can be morally valuable when it blocks rulers from treating residents as administrative property?
Do you agree that people are entitled to the products of their labor more strongly than to privileges created by law or conquest?
Do you agree that property claims lose moral force when they depend on exclusion without use, improvement, or consent?
Do you agree that private ownership of productive assets is legitimate only when titles do not originate in conquest or legal privilege?
Do you agree that correcting wealth created by legal privilege can be legitimate while ordinary personal possessions remain protected?
Do you agree that a property system should protect independence rather than making most people dependent on politically favored owners?
Do you agree that the legitimacy of property depends partly on whether others retain meaningful access to livelihood and exit?
Do you agree that in documented land-tenure systems, clear rules for possession, transfer, and dispute resolution can reduce overlapping claims?
Do you agree that large concentrations of ownership are easier to sustain when firms can convert political access into barriers against rivals?
Do you agree that in state-owned enterprises, public ownership changes the governance chain but does not by itself remove managerial hierarchy or accountability problems?
Do you agree that an ideal property regime should distinguish personal possessions from ownership or control of productive assets?
Do you agree that reform should target monopoly privilege, artificial scarcity, and title systems that block ordinary entry?
Do you agree that broad nationalization should not be treated as a cure for privilege unless governance incentives are solved first?
Do you agree that legal systems should make it easier for workers to form and govern worker-owned cooperatives?
Do you agree that policy should make ownership more contestable rather than merely moving control from private managers to public managers?
Do you agree that no property rule should be treated as sacred if it gives some people command over others without reciprocal obligation?
Do you agree that adults should be free to trade peacefully even when the resulting pattern is not what planners would choose?
Do you agree that economic planning is morally suspect when it treats people as instruments of a single collective blueprint?
Do you agree that economic coordination should respect plural ends rather than forcing one official hierarchy of social goals?
Do you agree that market outcomes deserve less deference when access to markets has been restricted by law or violence?
Do you agree that intervention is more legitimate when it removes privilege than when it substitutes officials' preferences for participants' choices?
Do you agree that the moral case for markets is strongest when entry, exit, and competition are real rather than nominal?

Do you agree that in market exchanges, prices can transmit some dispersed information without any participant knowing the whole economy, although market power and externalities can limit that function?
Do you agree that centralized planners may lack access to changing, local, or tacit information even when they are honest and technically competent?
Do you agree that regulated firms can possess technical information that regulators need, creating an information asymmetry that can increase capture risk?
Do you agree that an ideal economy would allow decentralized experimentation instead of one mandatory production plan?
Do you agree that competition policy should focus on removing barriers to entry before micromanaging prices or output?
Do you agree that where market failures are real, remedies should be narrow, transparent, and reversible?
Do you agree that when regulators are uncertain which business model will work, they should permit competing approaches unless a specific harm is demonstrated?
Do you agree that no one should have to justify every peaceful exchange to a political authority before acting?
Do you agree that a society should not tolerate destitution when preventing it would require only modest sacrifices from others?
Do you agree that material security matters because people without it are easier to dominate, not merely because they consume less?
Do you agree that aid should preserve agency rather than making recipients prove moral worth to administrators?
Do you agree that people harmed by state-created scarcity have stronger claims than people who merely lost ordinary market competition?
Do you agree that a welfare system becomes less legitimate when it conditions help on surveillance and humiliation?
Do you agree that the moral case for redistribution is stronger when the distribution being corrected was shaped by privilege?
Do you agree that, in a U.S. SNAP study, later recertification interview assignments reduced successful recertification and subsequent participation among affected cases?
Do you agree that an ideal safety net would secure basic agency while minimizing paternalistic supervision?
Do you agree that cash assistance should be favored over programs that force recipients into narrow approved consumption categories?
Do you agree that before adding new tax-funded benefits, governments should remove legal barriers that make essential goods and services unnecessarily expensive?
Do you agree that benefit rules should be designed to avoid cliffs that punish additional earnings?
Do you agree that local experimentation in welfare design should be permitted when recipients can exit bad programs?
Do you agree that no person should be forced into dependence on a boss, spouse, agency, or party to avoid starvation?
Do you agree that workers should be free to form organizations of their choice and bargain collectively without legal favoritism?
Do you agree that employment contracts are legitimate only when exit is meaningful and background rules are not rigged for employers?
Do you agree that a workplace is morally suspect when authority inside it is insulated from voice, exit, and competition?
Do you agree that state-backed union privilege is not automatically justified by employer power?
Do you agree that legal barriers that restrict workers’ ability to enter or leave employment can be forms of labor-market coercion?
Do you agree that in the U.S. occupations studied, licensing increased wages for licensed workers while reducing employment, with effects varying by occupation and model?

Do you agree that an ideal labor regime would extend basic legal protection to workers regardless of whether they are classified as employees, independent contractors, or members of a worker cooperative?
Do you agree that occupational-licensing requirements should be reduced when they block entry into ordinary jobs?
Do you agree that public-sector union rules should be stricter than private voluntary association because public services are coercively funded?
Do you agree that workers should control benefit accounts that remain theirs when they change employers?
Do you agree that worker-cooperative law should be simplified without forcing all firms into one ownership model?
Do you agree that labor policy should increase exit options before relying on mandatory bargaining structures?
Do you agree that no one has a right to use the state to prevent peaceful competitors from offering their labor?
Do you agree that no person created land, so exclusive claims to its unimproved value require special justification?
Do you agree that people should be free to build housing on their property when they do not impose concrete harms on others?
Do you agree that incumbent homeowners have weak moral claims to keep newcomers out to protect asset prices?
Do you agree that rent burdens caused by legal scarcity are a form of political extraction, not a neutral market fact?
Do you agree that the moral case for private landholding is strongest when land rents are not privately captured forever?
Do you agree that in high-cost metropolitan housing markets, permitting additional construction can moderate price pressure when land-use rules constrain supply?
Do you agree that in high-demand U.S. housing markets, zoning and other land-use controls can raise prices by restricting construction?
Do you agree that where housing supply is constrained, policy should remove barriers to apartments, accessory units, and mixed-use construction before broadly subsidizing demand?
Do you agree that a land-value tax should replace worse taxes where assessment institutions can be made credible?
Do you agree that tenant protection should not freeze the housing stock or make newcomers bear the full cost of scarcity?
Do you agree that infrastructure finance should capture rising land values rather than taxing unrelated activity?
Do you agree that excluding people from a high-opportunity location requires more justification than preserving a neighborhood aesthetic?
Do you agree that people should not be forced to use a politically privileged money when peaceful alternatives are available?
Do you agree that monetary institutions should not secretly redistribute purchasing power through opaque privilege?

Do you agree that saving, lending, and payment services should generally be open to new providers, subject to proportionate safeguards for capital, disclosure, consumer protection, and payment integrity?
Do you agree that bailouts are least legitimate when losses are socialized after gains were privatized?
Do you agree that financial stability does not justify permanent favoritism toward incumbent banks?
Do you agree that the legitimacy of money depends on consent, transparency, and protection from political manipulation?
Do you agree that competitive currencies can discipline issuers when users can switch at low cost?

Do you agree that because households differ in asset ownership, borrowing constraints, income sources, and labor-market exposure, monetary policy can affect them unevenly in ways policymakers cannot fully target?
Do you agree that in financial-sector licensing and compliance, uniform requirements can burden smaller entrants more than established firms with dedicated compliance capacity?
Do you agree that an ideal monetary order would allow competing monies, transparent reserves, and no privileged issuer?
Do you agree that payment innovation should not require discretionary permission from agencies aligned with incumbent banks?
Do you agree that bank-resolution rules should protect insured depositors while allocating losses to shareholders and unsecured or uninsured creditors before public funds?

Do you agree that people should generally be free to hold and use private, foreign, or digital currencies, subject to rules addressing fraud, insolvency, consumer protection, and payment-system stability?
Do you agree that central-bank emergency powers should be narrow, disclosed, and automatically sunset?
Do you agree that financial regulation should target fraud and insolvency rather than protecting established intermediaries from competition?
Do you agree that a money monopoly is not morally neutral merely because it is administered by experts?
Do you agree that copying information is not morally equivalent to taking a rival physical object?

Do you agree that creators should ordinarily receive attribution, but legal control over downstream uses should be limited when it would unnecessarily restrict criticism, research, repair, or follow-on creation?
Do you agree that using copyright to block repair, archiving, or interoperability is especially hard to justify?
Do you agree that patent claims are weaker when independent inventors would likely discover the same thing soon?
Do you agree that the strongest case for information control is fraud prevention, not artificial scarcity?
Do you agree that in some digital markets, open and interoperable standards can reduce switching or integration barriers?
Do you agree that in patent-intensive sectors, portfolios can be used for cross-licensing and litigation leverage as well as for protecting inventions, potentially affecting entry and competition?
Do you agree that an ideal information regime would protect attribution and fraud remedies without broad copying monopolies?
Do you agree that patent policy should narrow patent exclusivity—through shorter terms, narrower claims, or broader exceptions—before expanding enforcement remedies?
Do you agree that copyright exceptions for repair, archiving, research, remix, and interoperability should be broad?
Do you agree that publicly funded research should be released under open-access terms by default?
Do you agree that anti-circumvention law should not override ordinary ownership of devices people bought?
Do you agree that information policy should favor interoperable, open protocols and licensing that preserves follow-on use over broad exclusionary enforcement?
Do you agree that a society that criminalizes ordinary sharing has confused monopoly privilege with justice?
Do you agree that rights are most important when the speaker, religion, association, or defendant is unpopular?
Do you agree that the state should not decide which peaceful opinions are too dangerous for adults to hear?
Do you agree that privacy is a precondition for dissent, experimentation, and minority life?
Do you agree that fear of bad ideas does not justify giving officials a general censorship power?
Do you agree that due process should protect guilty and innocent people alike?
Do you agree that civil liberty should be treated as a constraint on politics, not as a benefit granted by current majorities?
Do you agree that emergency-law frameworks use sunset clauses, renewal limits, and periodic review because exceptional powers can persist beyond the conditions that prompted them?

Do you agree that an ideal rights regime would protect core civil liberties by default, requiring any restriction on expression, association, religion, encryption, or due process to satisfy a specific, publicly justified legal test?
Do you agree that restrictions on speech should require direct connection to fraud, threat, harassment, or specific rights violation?
Do you agree that surveillance powers should require adversarial warrants and meaningful notice after secrecy expires?
Do you agree that emergency limits on assembly or movement should sunset automatically unless reauthorized under strict review?
Do you agree that platforms should disclose state requests to remove or suppress lawful speech?
Do you agree that emergency surveillance powers should face the same judicial review regardless of which party controls government?
Do you agree that the right to be wrong is part of political equality?
Do you agree that punishment should require more justification than restitution, restraint, or repair?
Do you agree that a person does not forfeit all rights because they are accused or convicted of a crime?
Do you agree that victims deserve repair, not merely symbolic suffering imposed on offenders?
Do you agree that laws that create victimless crimes are morally weaker than laws against force and fraud?
Do you agree that state violence deserves stricter scrutiny because its victims cannot legally opt out?
Do you agree that public safety does not justify unlimited discretion for police, prosecutors, or prison officials?
Do you agree that law-enforcement agencies can improve apparent performance by emphasizing countable activity measures over outcomes such as safety, trust, and perceived legitimacy?
Do you agree that when law-enforcement agencies can receive or spend forfeiture proceeds, the funding structure creates a potential resource incentive around seizures?

Do you agree that in plea-bargaining systems, the prospect of a substantially harsher outcome after trial can pressure some defendants—including some who maintain innocence—to accept a plea, although the size and direction of the effect vary by case and are difficult to estimate?
Do you agree that an ideal justice system should use incapacitation only when necessary to prevent serious harm?
Do you agree that qualified immunity and similar shields should be narrowed when officials violate clear rights?
Do you agree that pretrial detention should be limited to specific flight or danger findings, not inability to pay?
Do you agree that justice reform should reduce official discretion where oversight is weak?
Do you agree that a justice system that cannot admit its own errors is not morally entitled to irreversible punishments?
Do you agree that birthplace is a morally arbitrary basis for excluding peaceful people from work, housing, and association?
Do you agree that states should not restrict peaceful adults from crossing borders solely to improve their lives?
Do you agree that citizenship should not operate as hereditary ownership of opportunity?
Do you agree that natives do not have a permanent veto over newcomers merely because they arrived earlier?
Do you agree that border enforcement is harder to justify when it traps people under violence or extreme poverty?
Do you agree that a political community may preserve institutions, but not by treating outsiders as rightless threats?

Do you agree that in randomized intergroup-contact studies with outcomes measured at least one day later, most comparisons reported lower measured prejudice, but effect sizes varied by target group and evidence for durable reductions in adults’ racial or ethnic prejudice was limited?
Do you agree that in U.S. industry data, migration barriers were lower where business lobbies spent more and higher where labor unions were more influential?
Do you agree that an ideal order would allow peaceful migration without treating national borders as ownership claims?
Do you agree that work authorization should be broad and quick even when citizenship rules remain stricter?
Do you agree that lawful immigration pathways should expand even when housing and labor markets need time to adjust?
Do you agree that asylum systems should be simplified so legal status does not depend on years of administrative limbo?

Do you agree that interior immigration enforcement should prioritize serious violence and fraud over otherwise nonviolent violations of immigration status or work authorization, with due process protections?
Do you agree that a person's right to sell labor should not disappear at a line drawn by states?
Do you agree that national identity is legitimate as voluntary belonging, not as a claim to rule dissenters or exclude outsiders?
Do you agree that civic membership should be open to people who accept equal legal status, not restricted by blood or ancestry?
Do you agree that local self-government is valuable because it protects exit and pluralism, not because every local majority is just?
Do you agree that sovereignty is least defensible when used to protect rulers from criticism by their own subjects?
Do you agree that cultural continuity does not justify coercive assimilation of peaceful minorities?
Do you agree that a nation may be a community of memory without being a moral owner of persons inside its borders?
Do you agree that in paired studies of Indian cities, stronger interethnic civic associations were associated with less communal violence than mainly intraethnic networks?
Do you agree that an ideal order would allow layered identities: local, regional, national, and cosmopolitan?
Do you agree that secession should be judged by exit rights and minority protections, not only by majority sentiment?
Do you agree that sovereignty claims should not override basic civil liberties or peaceful migration?
Do you agree that decentralization should include safeguards against local caste, ethnic, or religious domination?
Do you agree that love of place is not a license to coercively freeze culture?
Do you agree that religious conviction deserves protection, but not political supremacy over nonbelievers or dissenters?
Do you agree that coercive civil laws should be justifiable to citizens without requiring them to accept one religious authority?
Do you agree that voluntary religious communities should be free to set internal norms when exit is real?
Do you agree that blasphemy, apostasy, and heresy should not be civil crimes?
Do you agree that state favoritism toward a religion is unjust even when that religion is culturally dominant?
Do you agree that freedom of religion includes freedom from religion-backed law?
Do you agree that in countries with an official or preferred religion, governments are more likely to restrict other religious groups than in countries without one?
Do you agree that an ideal legal regime would protect religious exercise and nonreligious dissent under the same civil liberty principle?
Do you agree that religious exemptions should protect peaceful practice without allowing coercion of third parties?
Do you agree that the state should not fund or enforce religious doctrine through education, family law, or speech restrictions?
Do you agree that faith-based organizations receiving public funds should not gain privileges unavailable to secular associations?
Do you agree that religious arbitration should be enforceable only when participation and exit are genuinely voluntary?
Do you agree that secular public institutions should limit state power over conscience rather than impose an official state doctrine?
Do you agree that conscience cannot be delegated to a legislature, priesthood, or expert committee?
Do you agree that adults should be free to choose household forms that do not rely on coercion or fraud?
Do you agree that gender norms are least legitimate when enforced by law rather than persuasion and association?
Do you agree that care work deserves social respect even when it is unpaid, informal, or outside market employment?
Do you agree that formal consent inside families is not enough when exit is blocked by law, violence, or economic dependency?
Do you agree that the state should not enforce a single model of masculinity, femininity, marriage, or parenthood?
Do you agree that family policy should protect children and dependents without making peaceful adult difference illegal?
Do you agree that complex tax-transfer classifications can make eligibility and net benefits difficult for similarly situated households to predict?
Do you agree that family policy should expand adults’ ability to exit unwanted legal or economic dependency?
Do you agree that child welfare intervention should target concrete abuse or neglect, not mere deviation from dominant culture?
Do you agree that caregiver support should avoid locking people into dependency on either employers or spouses?
Do you agree that policy should expand real options rather than prescribing whether liberation means market work, domestic work, or communal care?
Do you agree that a role chosen freely is different from the same role imposed by law or economic captivity?
Do you agree that inherited group status should not determine legal standing, political rights, or access to opportunity?
Do you agree that a just society would not require cultural uniformity as the price of equal citizenship?
Do you agree that anti-domination matters more than symbolic diversity alone?
Do you agree that historical injustice can create present claims even when no current individual chose the original wrong?
Do you agree that collective guilt is a poor substitute for identifying institutions that still restrict people?
Do you agree that an ideal legal order would combine equal individual rights with freedom for voluntary cultural association?

Do you agree that anti-discrimination enforcement should focus on conduct and barriers, not compelled ideological rituals?
Do you agree that school and housing reform should attack exclusionary boundaries that reproduce inherited advantage?
Do you agree that no ancestry group has a natural right to rule, exclude, or be ruled?
Do you agree that future nonhuman life has moral standing even when protecting it does not benefit humans now?
Do you agree that nonhuman life deserves more than whatever price current owners can extract from it?
Do you agree that the natural world has moral standing even when protecting it would reduce long-run human prosperity?
Do you agree that polluters should not be allowed to impose diffuse harms merely because victims are hard to organize?
Do you agree that environmental policy loses legitimacy when it protects incumbent firms rather than ecological goods?
Do you agree that under CERCLA/Superfund, identifying a liable party can trigger a cleanup obligation or recovery of cleanup costs?
Do you agree that environmental regulations can alter competitive conditions when compliance costs vary by establishment or firm size?
Do you agree that an ideal environmental order would internalize harms without giving planners open-ended control over all production?
Do you agree that climate policy should reduce legal barriers to deploying low-carbon technologies and infrastructure?
Do you agree that pollution rules should be technology-neutral unless a specific technology creates unique risks?
Do you agree that conservation policy should compensate genuine stewardship and punish demonstrated harm, not merely signal virtue?
Do you agree that environmental subsidies should include sunset clauses and anti-capture review?
Do you agree that climate policy should prioritize reducing carbon and material intensity through technology and efficiency rather than broad consumption limits?
Do you agree that a clean environment is not a luxury good reserved for those who can buy distance from pollution?
Do you agree that political borders do not make foreign civilians morally less important than domestic civilians?
Do you agree that a state has no right to use its population as instruments of prestige, empire, or ideological crusade?
Do you agree that defensive force is easier to justify than projects of regime transformation abroad?
Do you agree that war powers should be distrusted most when officials claim urgency prevents scrutiny?
Do you agree that conscription is forced labor even when the cause is popular?

Do you agree that a person should be able to communicate privately without proving innocence first?
